topics.title: Earth–Sun relationship and heating
lesson: The Sun is the energy source for the atmosphere. How much of that energy reaches a place depends on the angle of the Sun's rays and the length of day, and both are set by Earth's axial tilt.

list: Earth's axis is tilted by an average of 23.5 degrees (NWS). NOAA/NESDIS gives 23.45 degrees from the perpendicular to the orbital plane. The tilt varies between about 22 and 24.5 degrees over long periods.
The axis keeps pointing the same way as Earth orbits, so each hemisphere leans toward the Sun for part of the year.

Distance is not the cause. Earth is closest to the Sun (perihelion) in January and farthest (aphelion) in July, when the Northern Hemisphere has summer. The distance difference is too small to explain the seasons.
Summer: the Sun's rays strike more directly, there is less atmospheric scattering, and days are long. Winter: the Sun is lower, and days are short.
June 21, summer solstice (Northern Hemisphere): the Sun is directly over the Tropic of Cancer, 23.5 N.
September 21 and March 21, equinoxes: the Sun is directly over the equator. Energy is balanced between hemispheres.
December 21, winter solstice (Northern Hemisphere): the Sun is directly over the Tropic of Capricorn, 23.5 S.
Equator: about 12 hours all year.
Mid-latitudes, such as South Dakota: about 15 hours near the summer solstice and about 9 near the winter solstice.
Arctic Circle (66.5 N): the Sun does not set from early June to early July, and there are only about 2 hours of daylight near the winter solstice.
North Pole: six months of daylight and six of darkness.
Radiation: transfer of heat through space by electromagnetic radiation. Sunlight warms the surface, and the surface radiates heat back into the atmosphere.
Conduction: transfer of heat from one substance to another or within a substance. Air conducts heat poorly.
Convection: transfer of heat in a fluid. Warmed surface air rises as a bubble warmer than its surroundings, cools as it rises, and cooler, denser air moves in below. That flow is felt as wind.
Dark surfaces such as asphalt absorb energy faster but also radiate it faster.

lesson.note: The NOAA heat transfer page does not cover advection (horizontal transport of heat by the wind) or latent heat. See the Wind and Moisture topics.

terms: Angle between Earth's rotation axis and the perpendicular to its orbital plane: about 23.5 degrees.
Closest approach to the Sun. Early January.
Farthest point from the Sun. Early July.
Date when the Sun is directly over 23.5 N or 23.5 S (about June 21 and December 21).
Date when the Sun is directly over the equator (about March 21 and September 21).

topics.title: Dew point and relative humidity calculations
lesson: Dew point and relative humidity both describe how close the air is to saturation. This topic shows how to move between them. The Moisture and Foundations topics give the physical picture.

list: Dew point: the temperature at which dew, or condensation, forms as a gas is cooled. If the condensate is ice it is called the frost point.
Relative humidity (RH): the ratio of the water vapour actually in the air (vapour pressure e) to the amount at saturation (es) at the same temperature and pressure. RH (%) = e / es x 100.
Dew point depression: air temperature minus dew point. Zero means the air is saturated (RH 100%).

lesson: There is no simple, direct formula to convert dew point to RH. You go through vapour pressures: the vapour pressure of the air is the saturation vapour pressure at the dew point, and RH compares that with the saturation vapour pressure at the air temperature.

lesson.formula: ln es(t) = ln 611.2 + 17.62 t / (243.12 + t), t in degrees C, es in Pa

lesson: Worked results from this formula (rounded): at 20 C, es is about 23.3 hPa. T 20 and Td 10: RH about 53%. T 15 and Td 15: RH 100%. T 10 and Td 5: RH about 71%. T 25 and Td 20: RH about 74%.

The Magnus formula is an approximation. NPL also gives the more accurate Sonntag (1990) equations, which need iteration when going from vapour pressure back to dew point. Over ice the Magnus constants are 22.46 and 272.62.

lesson.note: At a given dew point, RH rises as the air cools and falls as it warms, because es falls as the temperature falls. In practice the observer reads a psychrometer or a hygrometer and uses tables; this is the underlying calculation.

terms: Temperature to which air must be cooled for condensation to begin.
Dew point when the condensate is ice.
Ratio of actual vapour pressure to saturation vapour pressure at the same temperature and pressure, in percent.
Approximation for saturation vapour pressure as a function of temperature.

topics.title: Illumination: sunrise, sunset and twilight
lesson: Illumination data tells you when it is light or dark. It matters for observing, flying and tactical planning.

Conventionally, sunrise and sunset are the times when the upper edge of the Sun's disk is on the horizon (US Naval Observatory). The calculation allows for the average atmospheric refraction at the horizon, 34 arcminutes. Refraction means the Sun is still visible after it has geometrically set.

list: Civil twilight: the centre of the Sun is geometrically 6 degrees below the horizon. The brightest stars and planets are visible, you can see the horizon and landscape, and artificial light is often not needed.
Nautical twilight: 12 degrees below. The horizon is still visible, so sailors can take star sightings. Detailed outdoor work needs artificial light.
Astronomical twilight: 18 degrees below. The sky is dark for most people. Faint extended objects such as galaxies need a fully dark sky.

lesson: Morning twilight starts when the Sun is at these angles below the horizon on its way up. Evening twilight ends when it reaches them on its way down.

Moonrise and moonset occur when the Moon's upper limb is tangent to a level, unobstructed horizon. The USNO definition uses the geometric zenith distance of the Moon's centre, 90.5666 degrees plus the Moon's apparent angular radius minus its horizontal parallax.

lesson.note: Check your own authority for what counts as night in an operational or flying rule. This topic gives the astronomical definitions only.

topics.title: Space weather
lesson: Space weather is changes in the space environment and geomagnetic storms caused by eruptions on the Sun (Natural Resources Canada). It affects technology on Earth and in space. Canada is among the countries most exposed, because it is close to the north magnetic pole and the auroral zone.

list: Solar flare: an intense burst of radiation from released magnetic energy.
Coronal mass ejection (CME): a large explosion that throws superheated plasma into interplanetary space.
Coronal hole: a region that releases high-speed plasma, which strengthens the solar wind.
Solar wind: a constant stream of charged particles moving at more than 1.5 million km/h, carrying part of the Sun's magnetic field.
Solar cycle: activity rises and falls on a roughly 11-year cycle. Geomagnetic storms are more frequent near solar maximum.
Geomagnetic storms disturb Earth's magnetosphere and induce electric currents in long conductors such as power lines and pipelines. In extreme cases, power grids can black out or collapse.
Charged particles guided by Earth's magnetic field produce the aurora.
HF radio fades or blacks out, and satellite and navigation systems can be degraded (NOAA scales).
G scale, geomagnetic storms, from the Kp index: G1 Kp 5, G2 Kp 6, G3 Kp 7, G4 Kp 8, G5 Kp 9.
S scale, solar radiation storms, from the flux of particles at 10 MeV or more: S1 is 10 and each level is ten times greater, up to S5 at 100,000.
R scale, radio blackouts, from the X-ray flare class: R1 M1, R2 M5, R3 X1, R4 X10, R5 X20.

lesson: Example effects: G1 gives weak grid fluctuations, minor satellite effects and aurora at high latitudes. G2 can bring high-latitude voltage alarms, HF fading and aurora down to New York and Idaho. G5 can mean grid collapse, transformer damage and HF unusable for one to two days. R3 is a wide-area HF blackout of about an hour on the sunlit side. R5 is a complete HF blackout on the whole sunlit side for hours. S3 to S5 affect high-latitude HF and navigation and endanger astronauts and satellites.

lesson.note: The G, S and R scales are NOAA's (US). Check Space Weather Canada for the Canadian products.
